claims.text: Edge dislocations are responsible for the high strength and strength retention of BCC NbTaTiV and CrMoNbV refractory high-entropy alloys.
Edge dislocations are responsible for the high hardness of refractory high-entropy alloys.
Edge dislocations, rather than screw dislocations, can govern plastic flow and strength in NbTaTiV and CrMoNbV BCC HEAs.
Plastic flow in conventional BCC elemental metals and dilute alloys is generally controlled by screw dislocations.
Cold deformation by room-temperature high-pressure torsion increases the density of edge dislocations in refractory HEAs.
High-pressure torsion preferentially increases edge dislocations relative to screw dislocations.
High-pressure torsion increases the spatial hindrance and pinning of edge dislocations.
Edge dislocations in refractory HEAs are pinned by intrinsic lattice distortion.
Atomic-size mismatch and lattice distortion elevate the energy barrier for edge-dislocation glide in refractory HEAs.
Increasing the edge-dislocation population raises resistance to plastic deformation because those dislocations encounter enhanced impediments to motion.
Five turns of room-temperature HPT will increase the fraction or density of edge dislocations relative to a solution-annealed baseline.
Five turns of room-temperature HPT will increase hardness relative to a solution-annealed baseline.
Five turns of room-temperature HPT will increase yield strength relative to a solution-annealed baseline.
The solution-annealed refractory HEA has a less-developed dislocation network than the HPT-processed state.
Screw-dominated dislocation motion governs deformation in the solution-annealed NbTaTiV or CrMoNbV baseline.
The solution-annealed baseline has lower hardness and strength than the HPT-processed state.
The proposed behavior is limited to significantly lattice-distorted, refractory BCC HEAs.
The proposed behavior requires temperatures low enough to avoid phase transformation or recrystallization.
Activation of twinning or phase transformation may make the proposed edge-dislocation mechanism inapplicable.
TEM and neutron diffraction can identify the edge-dislocation character associated with strength in the cited NbTaTiV and CrMoNbV alloys.

contradictions.description: The initial state is described as solution-annealed but also as 'as-cast (or annealed),' whereas the controlled comparison elsewhere specifically requires a solution-annealed baseline. As-cast and solution-annealed states are not interchangeable controls.
